# Notes on 2 Kings 22

**What I covered and what's missing:** I got verse-by-verse notes from Enduring Word (Guzik), Precept Austin, and the older commentaries collected on BibleHub and StudyLight (Gill, Ellicott, Pulpit, Barnes, Keil & Delitzsch, Henry, Clarke, Poole). I found nothing from Catholic or Orthodox sites (newadvent, catholic.com, oca.org), nothing specifically Lutheran, Methodist or Pentecostal, nothing on prosperity or word-of-faith readings, and nothing on vv. 15–17 beyond basic summaries. Those parts are left out. The only real disagreement between Protestant groups I found is about Huldah (v. 14).

---

**v. 1**
- Josiah became king at eight because his father Amon was assassinated. Guzik quotes Knapp: this fulfils the prophecy of the "man of God out of Judah" from about 300 years earlier (1 Kings 13:2). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-22/
- Kings often names the king's mother because she could have real influence at court. Some think this hints that someone gave the young Josiah godly guidance, since his father was wicked. Precept Austin also gives a timeline: began seeking God at 16, began purging idols at 20, the Book found at 26, died at 39. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-22-commentary

**v. 2**
- "Did what was right" describes his reign as a whole, not the boy at age eight. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-22/
- "Not to the right or the left" echoes the rule for kings in Deuteronomy 17:20. Precept Austin says Josiah is the only king described this way. His life was not perfect, but it had a clear direction. Konkel (quoted there) calls him "a second Moses." https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-22-commentary

**v. 3**
- **The order of events.** 2 Chronicles 34 says Josiah's reforms began in his 8th and 12th years. So, Precept Austin argues, most of the reform came *before* the Book was found. Dale Ralph Davis (quoted there) thinks Kings focuses on one year to give a flavour of the whole reign. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-22-commentary
- Wiseman (quoted by Guzik) suggests the Chronicler's two-stage order may reflect that writer's own emphases. Guzik adds that Josiah may have been copying King Jehoash's earlier temple repair (2 Kings 12). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-22/

**vv. 4–7**
- Josiah saw that the repair work needed both organisation and money, and he provided both. Guzik notes that Jeremiah was the son of a priest named Hilkiah (Jeremiah 1:1). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-22/
- By one homiletical commentary's count, the temple had been left to decay for about 250 years, since Jehoash. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/2-kings-22.html

**v. 8**
- **What was found.** Older Protestant writers mostly say it was the Law of Moses, the temple copy kept beside the ark (Deuteronomy 31:26). https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/2Ki/2Ki_022.cfm
  - Gill thinks it was the whole Pentateuch, possibly Moses' own original. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-kings/22-8.html
  - Keil says "*the* book" shows it was something already known. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_kings/22-8.htm
- Matthew Henry imagines Hilkiah crying "Eureka!" over a treasure that nearly perished. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Ki/2Ki_022.cfm
- Guzik's application: when God's Word is recovered and spread, revival follows. His example is Peter Waldo. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-22/
- Precept Austin lists the options (the whole Pentateuch, Deuteronomy, or curse passages like Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28). https://www.preceptaustin.org/2_kings_commentaries Its own view is at least Deuteronomy and possibly more, partly because of the great Passover that followed. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-22-commentary
- **Sources disagree on how settled this is.** A Ligonier devotional says scholars "universally agree" it was Deuteronomy. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/book-grieved-josiah Precept Austin argues for more than Deuteronomy (above).
- **Modern scholarship.** Bible Odyssey says many scholars link the book to Deuteronomy. https://www.bibleodyssey.org/glossary/book-of-the-law/
  - A bible.org article says the view most favoured by modern Old Testament scholars goes back to de Wette (1805) and Wellhausen: the book was recently written to promote the reform. https://bible.org/article/book-josiahs-reform
- **Conservative replies to that view.**
  - Barnes lists ways a forgery would have been detected. Keil calls the forgery theory a distortion of the text. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_kings/22-8.htm
  - D. A. Carson (quoted by Precept Austin) says the theory is "increasingly being dismissed." https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-22-commentary
  - A Themelios article on TGC, drawing on Lohfink, argues that 2 Kings 22–23 combines at least two sources, so the book may not have driven the centralising reforms. That would undercut the theory. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/themelios/article/the-date-of-deuteronomy-linch-pin-of-old-testament-criticism-part-2/

**vv. 9–10**
- Shaphan reports the money first and the book last, calling it just "a book." Guzik, quoting Knapp, sees this as a sign of how neglected the Word had become. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-22/
- The Pulpit Commentary thinks Shaphan probably read only enough to see how important it was. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_kings/22-8.htm

**v. 11**
- Tearing clothes expressed horror and deep conviction of sin. Guzik links this to revival history (Orr on 1859) and to the Spirit's work of conviction (John 16:8). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-22/
- Ligonier ties his grief to Deuteronomy 17:14–20, the law his fathers had failed to keep. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/book-grieved-josiah

**vv. 12–13**
- Josiah knew how to seek God, but conviction left him unsure what to do next. He accepted that Judah deserved judgment. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-22/
- The urgency shows a heart that put God's Word above national pride. https://biblehub.com/2_kings/22.htm

**v. 14**
- **Why Huldah?** Guzik: she was consulted because she was recognised as a prophetess, not for her own wisdom. He also quotes Dilday that her name means "mole" (Shaphan means "rock badger," Achbor means "mouse"). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-22/
- Several older writers suggest practical reasons. Jeremiah was probably at Anathoth, Zephaniah was perhaps young, and Huldah lived nearby. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_kings/22-14.htm
- **"The college" (KJV).** Gill notes the Targum reads it as a house of instruction. Other translations take it as the "Second Quarter" of the city. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/ncv/2-kings/22-14.html
- **The Protestant debate: Huldah and women in ministry.**
  - *Complementarian voices on TGC* say prophesying is not pastoring. One article: "A prophetess is not a pastor." https://ca.thegospelcoalition.org/columns/ad-fontes/can-women-be-prophets/ Another says Huldah prophesied privately to messengers, unlike Isaiah or Jeremiah's public preaching. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/complementarianism/
  - *A GTY blog post (Grace to You)* holds that Huldah gave infallible, Scripture-level prophecy, and that this does not undermine complementarianism. It disputes John Piper's view that New Testament prophecy is a lesser, fallible gift. https://www.gty.org/blogs/B140317/fallibility-and-female-prophets
  - *Gavin Ortlund (TGC)* warns complementarians not to mute women's gifts, and cites Huldah. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/four-dangers-for-complementarians/
  - *Baker's Evangelical Dictionary* says the evidence is ambiguous enough to leave room for both complementarian and egalitarian views. https://www.studylight.org/dictionaries/eng/bed/w/woman.html
  - *A TGC (Themelios) review* rejects the claim, accepted in the book it reviews, that Huldah was "arguably the first" to give the Torah scroll authoritative status. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/themelios/review/recovering-from-biblical-manhood-and-womanhood-how-the-church-needs-to-rediscover-her-purpose/

**vv. 15–17**
- Judgment on Jerusalem is fixed because the people abandoned God and worshipped other gods. Even so, humble repentance moves God to spare Josiah from seeing it. https://biblehub.com/2_kings/22.htm
- Bible Odyssey: her prophecy helped spur vast religious reforms. https://www.bibleodyssey.org/dictionary/huldah/

**vv. 18–19**
- Guzik: Josiah's heart was tender both to God's Word, receiving the Spirit's conviction, and to Huldah's word of judgment. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-22/
- Pulpit: had the whole nation repented like this, it would likely have been spared too, because God never rejects a contrite heart. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-22.html

**v. 20 — "in peace," though Josiah later died in battle (2 Kings 23:29)**
- **About the timing, not the manner, of his death (Henry):** he died before the Babylonian captivity. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_kings/22-20.htm
- **Agrees in spirit, not in wording (Barnes):** the real threat came from Babylon, not Egypt. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_kings/22-20.htm
- **The phrase can include violent death (Keil):** "gathered to his fathers" is used even of kings slain in battle. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_kings/22-20.htm
- **Other explanations:**
  - Clarke: he was wounded but died in Jerusalem, at peace with God. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-kings/22-20.html
  - Pulpit: he was buried in his own land, not dragged into exile. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-22.html
  - Maclaren: the threats he asked about did not fall in his lifetime. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/maclaren_alexander/expositions-of-holy-scripture/2-kings/rediscovered-law-and-its-effects.cfm
  - Guzik gives three ways the promise held, including that he died before the exile. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-22/
- **Critical view:** Coffman reports that critics see a contradiction, multiple sources, or a later editor here. He rejects this and follows Keil. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-kings/22-20.html
